keyVerseText: Yet because this widow troubleth me, I will avenge her, lest by her continual coming she weary me.
rootMeaning: The word ὑπωπιάζω (hypōpiázō) derives from a compound of ὑπό (under) and a derivative of ὀπτάνομαι (to see), literally meaning to strike under the eye. This root sense conveys a vivid image of a physical blow causing a black eye, which extends metaphorically to the idea of persistent annoyance or subduing. The literal sense of striking beneath the eye enriches the English glosses by emphasizing a targeted, penetrating form of pressure or discipline rather than a general or vague weariness.
usageInScripture: This verb occurs only twice in the New Testament and is translated primarily as 'she weary' and 'I keep under,' highlighting two related but distinct nuances. In Luke 18:5, it describes the persistent annoyance caused by continual coming, while in 1 Corinthians 9:27 it carries the sense of self-discipline or subduing one's passions. The limited occurrences show the word’s consistent theme of exerting pressure—whether externally by others or internally by oneself—revealing a spectrum from irritation to intentional control.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding ὑπωπιάζω deepens our grasp of spiritual perseverance and discipline in the Christian life. The imagery of being struck under the eye or kept under control points to the reality of both external trials and internal self-mortification that believers face. It reminds us that faith involves enduring persistent challenges and actively subduing sinful desires. This word encapsulates the tension between suffering and spiritual growth, encouraging believers to embrace discipline as a means of sanctification and reliance on God’s sustaining grace.
keyVerseReflection: Luke 18:5 states, 'Yet because this widow troubleth me, I will avenge her, lest by her continual coming she weary me.' Here, ὑπωπιάζω conveys the widow's persistent coming as a kind of pressure that could exhaust or annoy the judge. This word highlights the widow’s relentless faith and determination, which ultimately leads to justice. It teaches us that persistent faith, even when it feels burdensome, is powerful and effective before God.
